Thank you for resubmitting your work entitled "Long-term balancing selection drives evolution of immunity genes in Capsella" for further consideration at eLife. Your revised article has been favorably evaluated by Ian Baldwin (Senior Editor), a Reviewing Editor, and two reviewers.

The manuscript has been improved but there are some remaining issues with the presentation and discussion that need to be addressed before acceptance, as outlined below. Notably reviewer 2 made a number of useful suggestions of clarifications that would be helpful in understanding the analyses and results.

Reviewer #1:

This manuscript is significantly improved. However, the writing is still rough in several places, and there are some other things that should be improved.

The Abstract suggests that the study aim is "to understand the extent to which natural selection can drive the retention of genetic diversity", meaning sequence diversity. In fact, however, the conclusions relate mainly to whether genes whose sequences suggest that they are involved in resistance to pathogens show footprints of balancing selection, as has been suggested many times, and for which there is some empirical evidence, including from analyses of diversity. This study is therefore an advance mainly in that such genes were not chosen for study and shown to have interesting diversity patterns, but instead they emerged from a genomic analysis for balancing selection, and specifically through analyzing shared polymorphisms.

The revised manuscript concludes that genes showing signals of potential balancing selection show an enrichment for genes involved in interactions with pathogens. I have two comments about this. First, are some of these genes located in clusters in physically small genome regions (as is commonly the case for plant NRR genes)? If so, could this over-estimate the fraction under balancing selection, because one gene is actually under balancing selection, and the others have correlated diversity patterns, due to close linkage? This would seem to be a particular concern for any clusters that are located in regions of low recombination, or low effective recombination rates (which could encompass considerable parts of the genomes of the selfing species studied).

It is far from clear that "self-fertilizing species provide increased sensitivity to detect balancing selection" (as claimed in the Introduction) and indeed the evidence is not compelling, though it is overall consistent with its having been detected in the selfing Capsella species studied. Moreover, only certain kinds of balancing selection could be detected in a selfer, notably situations involving frequency dependence (not heterozygote advantage). This claim should therefore not be made.

Second, the revised manuscript makes much clearer than before that the long-term balancing selection that may have been detected could potentially occur solely within the outcrossing species from which the selfing species evolved (in one case, apparently very recently). The signal within the selfing species might therefore not reflect ongoing selection in those species, but merely introgression of sequences bearing the footprints of the selection. The revised text marshalls the evidence on this question quite clearly. However, it is not mentioned that introgression by pollen flow into the selfing species is more likely than the reverse, following the long-established general rule for attempts to inter-cross two species when only one of them is self-incompatible: pollen of the self-compatible species often fails to work on pistils of the self-incompatible one, whereas the reciprocal pollination succeeds (as might be expected if selfing species' pistils have lost the ability to reject incompatible pollen). However, some recently evolved selfing species also reject pollen from their close self-incompatible relatives. A comment on the case in these Capsella species would be worth adding. In my opinion, the abstract should mention that tests for adaptive introgression suggest that this is not causing the signal(s) on which the conclusion of balancing selection in the selfers is based.

The first paragraph is poorly written and somewhat misleading, as it fails to mention that loss of alleles in situation with strong balancing selection occurs only in special cases. I think that the authors meaning is as follows. The term "balancing selection" describes several different adaptive forces that maintain genetic variation for longer than expected under genetic drift of neutral variants. It includes situations with heterozygous advantage, negative frequency-dependent selection (rare allele advantage), and environmental heterogeneity affecting fitnesses in space and time. In these situations, selection prevents loss of alleles from populations at the functional genes or sites. As this also results in increased diversity at closely linked neutral or weakly selected sites (Charlesworth, 2006), it should be possible to detect balancing selection from the resulting footprints of increased coalescence times at closely linked sites, and many candidate genes have been identified using diverse methodology (Fijarczyk and Babik, 2015). However, theoretical models predict that even strongly balanced functional alleles can be stochastically lost over long time periods, suggesting that balanced polymorphism could often be short lived [a reference is needed here], particularly when the functional alleles have low equilibrium frequencies, or fluctuate in frequency, with periods of low frequency, as may occur in the case of plant pathogen resistance genes where temporarily rare alleles may have advantages (Tellier et al., 2014). There is no need to repeat this reference in the Introduction. It would be better to make clear all along that this is a special case.

Reviewer #2:

The manuscript has been substantially improved after extensive revisions. Removal of the discussion of evolution of sex makes the main story much clearer, and I appreciate the explicit discussion of different possible mechanisms underlying the shared polymorphisms (technical artifacts, recurrent mutations, maintenance of ancestral variation, introgression, etc). The evidence of trans-species polymorphisms in MLO2b is very compelling, and I am convinced that the high-quality three-way tsSNPs show evidence for long-term balancing selection and no evidence of recent gene flow.

However, I have a few questions about the analysis and hope the authors could add some details in the manuscript to improve clarity. I also feel the current abstract is too vague and lacks specifics of some key results. For instance, it is unclear which collection of variants the authors are referring to when saying "ancestral variation preferentially persists at immunity related loci" (ts_2waySNPs, Bal regions, ts_3waySNPs, or ts_3wayhqSNPs?). In addition, the gene name MLO2b should be specified in the second to the last sentence, as this is the only case the authors demonstrate trans-species sharing of haplotypes clearly. Please see below for my specific questions and comments.

1) The authors use the D statistic and IBD sharing to support their conclusion of ongoing gene flow between C. grandiflora and eastern C rubella, but some details of these analyses are unclear.

D-statistic calculation:

1) What exactly is the configuration for the ABBA-BABA test. For example, what species is used as the outgroup?

2) Why is the correlation between D statistic and distance evidence for ongoing gene flow (as claimed in subsection “Capsella rubella demography”)? Could this reflect past gene flow?

IBD detection:

1) What does the minimum segment length of 1kb translate into genetic distance? I am not familiar with recombination rates in plants, but such segments seem very short by standards in humans and thus very old. (The length threshold is only specified in legend of Figure 2, but I think it should also be included in the Materials and methods section.)

2) What is the distribution of detected IBD segment lengths?

3) Can the authors provide some estimates for the age of the IBD segments based on their lengths to support their conclusion of "very recent co-ancestry"?

2) Figure 4 is one of the key results showing enrichment in immunity-related genes, but it is unclear what each panel shows exactly, as some details or labels are missing.

1) Panel A: What does each dot mean? I guess each point represents a gene, but this is not clear from the text, figure or legend. What is the y-axis in each sub-panel? How is this number calculated?

2) Panels B: what do the thick line and the shaded area mean, respectively? Does the legend of panel C apply to panel B?

3) The authors use simulation data to argue against the possibility that the diversity patterns near Bal loci result from historical balancing selection in the ancestor population. Did the simulations include effects of balancing selection? If so, how is balancing selection simulated in practice? If balancing selection is not simulated, are the results based on neutral simulations sufficient to rule out the possibility of historical balancing selection?

4) MLO2b region

1) Why is the haplotype structure of MLO2b not discussed on C grandiflora? Since the tsSNPs are shared by C grandiflora, it seems the selection pressure is preserved in this species. Would the higher recombination rate in C grandiflora help narrow down the causal variant(s)?

2) How long are the shared haplotypes between C rubella and C orientalis? Is maintenance of such long haplotypes expected, given plausible split time and recombination rate, if there is no epistasis? It will be helpful to estimate this using the formula in Wiuf et al., 2004.

3) Based on Figure 3B, haplogroup C differs by only 1 SNP from the second haplotype in group B. Why is C classified as the separate haplogroup instead of a subtype of B?

4) In subsection “Insights into balancing selection from de novoassembly of MLO2”, the authors concluded that the shared haplotypes did not result from recent gene flow, because of similar within-haplotype divergence levels of A and B haplogroups. However, this evidence is insufficient: the authors need to demonstrate that the within-haplogroup divergence is at least as high as the genome-wide average (which seems to be the case by comparing Figure 6—figure supplement 1 to Figure 5D).

5) The reconstructed trees in Figure 6C are very small, and haplotypes need to be labeled in order to show the pattern of clustering by haplogroup.

results.result: The study analyzed 50 C. rubella and 13 C. grandiflora accessions, applying stringent filters that resulted in 74% of the C. rubella reference genome remaining accessible. After filtering, 5,784,607 SNPs and 883,837 indels were identified, with 824,540 SNPs found in both species (tsCgCrSNPs), 4,291,959 segregating only in C. grandiflora, and 640,256 only in C. rubella. Sample rarefaction indicated that common SNP discovery was near saturation.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C46 describe the sample sizes, filtering approach, and variant discovery results. These are straightforward data reporting claims supported by the methods and results sections, with appropriate quality control measures described. The rarefaction analysis (C45, Figure 1D) validates the sampling adequacy.

results.result: C. rubella exhibits a dramatic reduction in genetic diversity consistent with a genetic bottleneck, with SNPs much less likely to be heterozygous than in C. grandiflora (though occasional outcrossing is observed). Linkage disequilibrium decayed to 0.1 within 5 kb in C. grandiflora but only at distances greater than 20 kb in C. rubella.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C51 describe expected population genetic consequences of selfing, supported by data in Figure 1E-F and citations to prior studies. The heterozygosity patterns and LD decay are consistent with the biology of selfing species and are well-documented.

results.result: Population structure analysis revealed three genetic clusters: one including all C. grandiflora individuals and C. rubella samples split into two clusters (West and East). The structure was strongly associated with geography, with samples from western Europe and southeastern Greece assigned to separate groups, while northern Greek samples showed mixed ancestry. This pattern is consistent with northern Greece being the center of diversity for C. rubella and a more recent expansion into Western Europe.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C58 describe population structure results from ADMIXTURE and PCA analyses (Figure 2A-B). The geographic patterns are clearly shown and the inference about the center of diversity and expansion is reasonable given the data and is supported by citation to prior work (C58).

results.result: Evidence for ongoing gene flow between C. rubella and C. grandiflora was found, including one C. grandiflora sample with partial C. rubella ancestry, eastern C. rubella individuals less differentiated from C. grandiflora, significant genome-wide D-statistics that decrease with distance from C. grandiflora's range, and IBD segments that decrease with distance. This is consistent with interspecific crosses producing fertile offspring.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C66 present multiple lines of evidence for gene flow (ADMIXTURE, PCA, D-statistics, IBD analysis) shown in Figure 2 and supplements. The convergence of multiple independent methods strengthens the conclusion. The inference of ongoing gene flow (C65) is well-supported by the data and consistent with cited experimental crosses (C66).

results.result: Demographic modeling estimated the split between C. rubella and C. grandiflora occurred 170,000 generations ago with a strong population size reduction in C. rubella (to 2-14 effective chromosomes). Bidirectional gene flow occurred until just over 10,000 generations ago when C. rubella split into W and E populations, after which gene flow continued only from E C. rubella to C. grandiflora. Assuming 1.3 years per generation, this corresponds to ~13,500 years ago, similar to the spread of agriculture and end of the last glaciation in Europe.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C75 describe demographic modeling results using fastsimcoal2 (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 2). The model fitting appears appropriate and the inference about timing and directionality of gene flow is supported by the data. The connection to historical events (C74-C75) is speculative but reasonable. The generation time assumption is justified by citation to a related species.

results.result: Over half of segregating variants in C. rubella were also found in C. grandiflora (tsCgCrSNPs), which are strongly enriched among high-frequency alleles in both species (p << 0.0001). At allele frequencies >0.25 in C. rubella, tsCgCrSNPs accounted for >80% of variation. These results indicate tsCgCrSNPs are predominantly older alleles present in the common ancestral population or introgressed prior to westward expansion.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C79 describe the derived allele frequency analysis (Figure 3A) showing that trans-specific SNPs are enriched at high frequencies. The statistical test is appropriate (Mann-Whitney U-test) and the inference about allele age (C79) is reasonable given the allele frequency patterns. This is a key finding supporting the retention of ancestral variation.

results.result: The distribution of tsCgCrSNPs was uneven across the genome. Compared to ssCrSNPs from the same allele frequency distribution, tsCgCrSNPs were less likely to result in nonsynonymous changes (p < 0.001) but more likely to be in genes. 83% of tsCgCrSNPs were in complete LD with at least one other tsCgCrSNP, and their density was highly variable, positively correlated with local genetic diversity in C. rubella and negatively correlated with Fst. The uneven pattern was similar in each C. rubella subpopulation, indicating most retained polymorphism segregated prior to colonization.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C90 describe the genomic distribution and characteristics of trans-specific SNPs (Figure 3B-J and supplements). The statistical analyses are appropriate (jackknife resampling, correlation analyses) and the inference that retained polymorphism predates colonization (C88) is well-supported by the similarity across subpopulations. This establishes the non-random retention of variation.

results.result: tsCgCrSNPs were strongly biased toward genes involved in plant biotic interactions, including defense and immune responses, and also toward pollen-pistil interactions. Top enriched GO categories included apoptotic process, defense response, innate immune response, programmed cell death, and defensive secondary metabolite production. 87% of genes annotated with apoptotic process were NLR gene homologs, and tsCgCrSNPs in NLR genes were more likely to result in nonsynonymous changes. Despite severe global loss of genetic diversity, genes involved in plant-pathogen interactions maintained high levels of genetic variation in C. rubella.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C97 describe GO enrichment analysis results (Figure 4A, Supplementary file 1) showing strong enrichment for immunity-related genes. The analysis appears appropriate and the conclusion (C97) is well-supported by the enrichment data. This is a central finding of the paper linking retained variation to immunity genes.

results.result: Quality control analyses showed that tsCgCrSNPs and ssSNPs had nearly identical distributions of coverage and concordance metrics, indicating mismapping is unlikely to have affected SNP calls. tsCgCrSNPs were not more likely to be heterozygous than ssSNPs. Elevated tsCgCrSNPs sharing and genetic diversity extended over 100 kb from NLR genes, and increased sharing is not an artifact of the internal structure of NLR clusters.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C101 address potential technical artifacts (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Figure 4B-C). The quality control analyses are appropriate and demonstrate that the enrichment of trans-specific SNPs near immunity genes is not due to technical issues. The analysis excluding NLR clusters themselves (C101) is particularly important for ruling out artifacts.

results.result: 21 genomic regions were identified as candidate targets of balancing selection (Bal regions) based on Fst analysis compared to neutral simulations. Bal regions showed substantially higher Tajima's D and within-C. rubella genetic diversity (p<<0.001), and tsCgCrSNPs in these regions were less likely to be lost during colonization with elevated allele frequency correlation across populations. Nine Bal regions overlapped with NLR gene clusters and five with RLK/RLP or CRK gene clusters. Many specific regions have been demonstrated to function in disease resistance in A. thaliana, and RPP1 and RPP8 have been previously suggested as balancing selection targets.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C113 describe the identification and characterization of balanced regions (Figure 4D-F, Figure 4—source data 1). The simulation-based approach for identifying outlier regions is appropriate, and the multiple lines of supporting evidence (Tajima's D, diversity, allele frequency patterns) strengthen the conclusion. The overlap with known immunity genes from A. thaliana (C111-C113) provides independent validation.

results.result: The strongest signals of balancing selection are mostly derived from linked sites rather than the clusters themselves, because confident SNP calling is very difficult with short reads in complex genomic regions. Genetic diversity was only modestly elevated in Bal regions in C. grandiflora (p<<0.001) and Tajima's D was not significantly different from other windows. Even accounting for elevated founder diversity, observed Fst values in Bal regions remain exceptionally unlikely under neutral simulations (p<0.0001), pointing to ongoing balancing selection within C. rubella.
results.evaluation: Claims C114-C119 address alternative explanations and provide evidence for ongoing selection in C. rubella rather than just historical selection in C. grandiflora (Figure 4E-F, Figure 4G). The simulation-based test accounting for elevated founder diversity (C118) is particularly important for ruling out neutral explanations. The conclusion of ongoing selection (C119) is well-supported.

results.result: A larger fraction of Bal region sequence was IBD compared to the genome-wide average, but shared segments in Bal regions were shorter (median 3,503 bp vs 6,661 bp, p=1e-54), suggesting they are older. Within the East population, IBD in Bal regions decayed with distance from C. grandiflora's range similarly to the genome-wide pattern but with a shallower slope. High levels of IBD were observed between C. grandiflora and West population accessions in Bal regions, contrasting with the genome-wide pattern. This is consistent with alleles being introgressed prior to range expansions and subsequently maintained by selection.
results.evaluation: Claims C120-C125 describe IBD patterns in balanced regions (Figure 4—figure supplement 2). The analysis of IBD segment lengths and geographic patterns provides evidence for the timing and maintenance of introgressed alleles. The inference (C125) is reasonable given the data, though the alternative explanation of differing recombination patterns is acknowledged in the text.

results.result: Selfing evolved independently in C. orientalis, which diverged from C. grandiflora and C. rubella over 1 million years ago and whose modern range no longer overlaps with the other species. The study resequenced 16 C. orientalis genomes, identifying only 71,454 segregating SNPs, corresponding to an almost 50-fold reduction in diversity relative to C. grandiflora. C. orientalis diverged from C. grandiflora over 1.8 million generations ago. Using population genetics calculations, the probability of finding a single tsSNP by chance is <4×10^-19.
results.evaluation: Claims C126-C132 establish the independent evolution of selfing in C. orientalis and the extremely low probability of finding trans-specific SNPs by chance. The divergence time estimates and probability calculations are based on established methods (cited) and the data. This sets up the key test of long-term balancing selection.

results.result: Despite the extremely low probability, 8,408 C. orientalis variants were shared with either C. rubella or C. grandiflora (ts2-waySNPs) and 3,992 with both (ts3-waySNPs). In each species, ts3-waySNPs were enriched at higher derived allele frequencies relative to ssSNPs and ts2-waySNPs. After stringent filtering, 812 high quality three-way trans-specific SNPs (ts3-wayhqSNPs) were identified, with distributions of coverage and concordance values similar to other C. orientalis sites.
results.evaluation: Claims C133-C137 report the surprising finding of trans-specific SNPs across all three species (Figure 5A-C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1). The stringent filtering approach and quality control analyses (C137) address potential concerns about false positives. The enrichment at high frequencies (C135) supports the interpretation that these are old, maintained alleles.

results.result: In all three species, diversity was high directly adjacent to ts3-wayhqSNPs, close to average levels for genome-wide divergence between the two Capsella lineages. The footprint of elevated diversity is much more discernible in the two selfing species than in C. grandiflora. No obvious reduction in divergence was observed near ts3-wayhqSNPs. These results indicate ts3-wayhqSNPs correspond predominantly to long-term maintained alleles that diverged on ancient time scales and are not the result of recent introgression.
results.evaluation: Claims C138-C141 describe diversity and divergence patterns around three-way trans-specific SNPs (Figure 5D). The analysis appropriately distinguishes between recent introgression (which would reduce divergence) and long-term maintenance (which would not). The conclusion (C141) is well-supported by the data.

results.result: Minor alleles at ts3-wayhqSNP sites are closer to intermediate frequencies in all three species compared to ts2-waySNPs. ts3-wayhqSNPs segregate at more similar allele frequencies in C. rubella and C. grandiflora than other two-way tsSNPs (median Fst 0.03 vs 0.16, p<<0.001), suggesting a conserved equilibrium maintained since isolation over 10,000 generations ago. However, derived allele frequencies for ts3-wayhqSNPs are not correlated between the two ancient Capsella lineages (Spearman's rho -0.08 and -0.04), possibly due to demographic reduction or habitat shift in C. orientalis.
results.evaluation: Claims C142-C146 describe allele frequency patterns at three-way trans-specific SNPs (Figure 5—figure supplement 2, Figure 4—source data 2). The similar frequencies in C. rubella and C. grandiflora (C143) support a conserved equilibrium, while the lack of correlation with C. orientalis (C145) is acknowledged with a reasonable speculative explanation (C146).

results.result: ts3-waySNPs are strongly enriched in GO categories associated with immunity. 50% of ts3-wayhqSNPs fell into the previously identified balanced regions (which encompass <10% of tsCgCrSNPs and <3% of all SNPs). At least one ts3-wayhqSNP was found in 10 of the 21 original candidate balanced regions: six corresponding to NLR clusters, two to RLK/RLP clusters, and one to a TIR-X cluster. Even where a genetic bottleneck has wiped out almost all genetic diversity, there is very strong selection to maintain allelic diversity at specific immunity-related loci, consistent with these alleles having persisted for very long evolutionary times.
results.evaluation: Claims C147-C154 show the remarkable overlap between three-way trans-specific SNPs and previously identified balanced regions (Figure 5F-G, Supplementary file 2). The 50% overlap (C148) is highly significant given the small fraction of the genome these regions represent. This provides strong evidence for long-term balancing selection at immunity loci. The conclusion (C153-C154) is well-supported.

results.result: A homolog of A. thaliana MLO2 was selected for detailed analysis. MLO2 encodes a seven-transmembrane domain protein with a conserved role in plant disease susceptibility. The C. rubella MLO2 locus has a tandem duplication resulting in MLO2a and MLO2b, with all six ts3-wayhqSNPs in MLO2b. In C. rubella and C. orientalis, the ts3-wayhqSNPs were arranged in five haplotypes collapsed into three haplogroups (A, B, C). Haplogroup B in both species exhibited similar patterns of low read coverage at the 5' end of MLO2b.
results.evaluation: Claims C155-C160 introduce the MLO2 case study (Figure 6, Supplementary file 3). The selection criteria are clearly stated and the initial characterization of the locus structure and haplotypes is straightforward data reporting. The observation of low coverage in haplogroup B (C160) sets up the subsequent analysis.

results.result: The pattern of low coverage for haplogroup B at MLO2b was not due to structural variation but to extremely high divergence from reference haplogroup A. Divergence between alleles within species was >0.15 differences per bp, over three times higher than genome-wide divergence between species. De novo assembly identified 204 additional tsSNPs, nearly all mapping to the 5' end of MLO2b. Neighbor-joining trees revealed expected clustering by species in adjacent regions but clear clustering by haplogroup within the 5' region.
results.evaluation: Claims C161-C165 describe the de novo assembly analysis of MLO2b (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1-2). This is a key methodological contribution showing that reference-based approaches miss highly divergent alleles. The phylogenetic analysis (C165) confirms the trans-specific nature of the haplotypes. The divergence levels (C162-C163) are striking and well-documented.

results.result: Divergence within haplogroup across species at MLO2b was greater than or similar to genome-wide averages for both A and B, demonstrating that recent introgression did not give rise to allele sharing. In a 157 amino acid stretch, 31 amino acid differences are found between haplogroups A and B in both species, with an indel accounting for another seven amino acid differences. The large number of differences makes it difficult to identify specific targets of selection, but it seems likely the two haplogroups differ functionally. The nucleotide divergence suggests the MLO2b haplogroups are much older than the split between the two species.
results.evaluation: Claims C166-C171 complete the MLO2b analysis (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1, 3). The divergence analysis (C166) rules out recent introgression, and the protein-level differences (C168-C169) are substantial. The inference of functional differences (C170) is reasonable though speculative. The conclusion about ancient divergence (C171) is well-supported by the data.

results.result: Ancestral variation preferentially persists at immunity-related loci in Capsella after species-wide bottlenecks, and the same collection of alleles has been maintained in different lineages separated for several million years. The data point to long-term balancing selection as an important factor shaping the genetics of immune systems in plants and as the predominant driver of genomic variability after a population bottleneck.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C4, C7, C8 represent the main conclusions of the paper. These are well-supported by the multiple lines of evidence presented: enrichment of trans-specific SNPs at immunity loci (C91-C97), identification of balanced regions (C102-C113), three-way trans-specific SNPs in C. orientalis (C133-C154), and the MLO2b case study (C155-C171). The convergence of evidence from multiple independent analyses strongly supports these conclusions.

results.result: Divergence between ancient haplotypes can be obscured by reference-based re-sequencing methods, and trans-specific alleles can encode substantially diverged protein sequences. The detection of long-term balancing selection is further compounded by very old alleles being less accessible to short read re-sequencing.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C6, C173 describe an important methodological finding demonstrated by the MLO2b case study. The de novo assembly revealed 204 additional trans-specific SNPs and extreme divergence (>0.15 differences per bp) that was missed by reference-based mapping. This is a significant technical contribution with implications for other studies of balancing selection.

results.result: Balancing selection likely plays a similar role in other taxa but its effects are masked by higher neutral diversity and more frequent recombination. In selfing Capsella species, footprints of balancing selection extend for tens of kilobases, improving statistical power to detect causal regions but reducing ability to identify specific variants. Stable balancing selection in selfing species is unlikely to derive from heterozygous advantage, pointing to environmental heterogeneity or negative frequency-dependent selection. Based on enrichment of immunity-related genes, biotic factors appear to be the dominant drivers of long-term maintenance of polymorphism.
results.evaluation: Claims C172, C174-C178 discuss the implications and mechanisms of balancing selection. The speculation about other taxa (C172) is reasonable given the findings. The observation about extended LD in selfers (C174-C175) is well-supported by the data (Figure 1F, Figure 4B-C). The inference about mechanisms (C176-C177) is logical given the biology of selfing. The conclusion about biotic factors (C178) is strongly supported by the GO enrichment analyses.

results.result: The observations are consistent with a large body of work on intraspecific variation in A. thaliana, where balancing selection has been observed for specific disease resistance alleles, and alternative RPS5 alleles affect fitness in the field. The signal of balancing selection may be amplified by immunity-related loci occurring in clusters, and the clustering itself may be a product of selection.
results.evaluation: Claims C179-C183 place the findings in the context of prior work on A. thaliana. The consistency with prior literature (C179-C181) is supported by appropriate citations. The speculation about clustering (C182-C183) is reasonable and acknowledges uncertainty, with appropriate citations to relevant concepts.

results.result: The findings suggest a model in which the success of self-fertilizing populations may be buoyed by gene flow from outcrossing relatives, analogous to evolutionary rescue strategies. This is a variation on adaptive introgression, which has emerged as a major evolutionary force in many taxa. Constant replenishment via adaptive introgression from an outcrossing relative counters the loss of diversity at immunity-related loci, preventing decreased fitness in competition with pathogens.
results.evaluation: Claims C184-C186 propose a model based on the findings. The model is reasonable given the evidence for gene flow (C59-C66), preferential retention of introgressed alleles in balanced regions (C120-C125), and maintenance of diversity at immunity loci. Identification of useful immunity-related polymorphism with genomic data might be facilitated in otherwise homogeneous wild populations.
results.evaluation: Claims C187-C189 discuss potential applications of the findings. The observation about detectability (C187) is supported by the study's success in identifying balancing selection in low-diversity selfing species. The speculation about applications (C188-C189) is reasonable but remains untested. These are appropriate forward-looking statements.
